S2's -50 suffix drop is 5 ccr plus 45 bare sr forms under the same defaulting rule, all nine spellings byte-checked. DECODER COVERAGE measured on both sides: master recognises 42,774 of 65,536 words, the branch 44,337, and the +1,563 was DERIVED BEFORE master was measured and agrees exactly. VERIFIED HERE: landing run 378 suites / 4,366 passed / 0 failed / 2 ignored, zero skip:/ratchet:/FAILED, exit 0, reconciling master's 4,362 + four new tests; the trailing commit is docs-only, filtered here; no file overlap with master's own move; clippy re-run BY ME at exit 0; aeon's four shapes byte-identical, re-measured by me. Golden vectors 114 -> 176 with all 114 existing byte-identical, AS snippets 193 -> 201 with zero churn in the 193. Red-first proof for the bare-suffix rule with the mutation shown applied and THE BINARY REBUILT on restore. TWO BRIEF CORRECTIONS: the 58-site figure is right for the five instructions but I framed it against a 9,739 baseline that is now 368; and my S1 framing implied S2 needed nothing here, when S2 carries 73 sites of the same five. OPEN: the label-on-if binding; the cycle table prices none of the five, resolving to Unknown which is the loud direction; usp and move-to-ccr deliberately not exposed in .emp, since a new operand kind is language surface and the owner's call.

headline: Sonic 1 already comes out of our assembler at 98.6% of the real cartridge - and the single biggest thing still missing is not the assembler's job at all.
matters: The honest framing first: 318 complaints reads like a wall, and it is not one. Stand in for the constructs our frontend still refuses - rewriting them into forms it already supports, so the assembler still computes every byte itself - and it exits cleanly and writes 524,288 bytes, exactly retail size, of which 517,003 are byte-for-byte the real Sonic 1. Seven regions differ and every one has a named cause. The most useful discovery is in the largest of those regions, and it reshapes what this project's finishing line even means: the retail build does not come out of the assembler. A second tool runs afterwards and COMPRESSES part of the finished image - the sound driver - and pads the gaps with a different filler byte than we use. That is 82% of everything still differing, it is work no assembler does, and I verified it from the disassembly's own build script rather than taking the agent's word. So replacing the assembler is necessary and NOT sufficient to produce the cartridge, and the milestone row that assumed otherwise has been corrected. Second: the complaint count was blind to progress, not just to danger. Third, and cheapest: the best next fix is one line. A label sharing its line with a conditional is silently dropped; that single site is worth 13 complaints AND is the sole cause of all 16 failures at the linking stage. It was already on the board.
detail: Landed at master 5cbcc789 (merge of the S1 measurement parcel, tip d2c32940), pushed and verified by ls-remote. Seventeenth landing. Note: docs/superpowers/notes/2026-09-04-s1-path-to-rom.md (445 lines) plus reproducible probes under .s1probe/2026-09-04/. NO sigil source changed - crates/ diff is empty, so no gate could be affected and no suite run was owed. PROVENANCE: sigil 7bef76e6; corpus s1disasm f6ece657 in two pristine detached worktrees (the LIVE s1disasm checkout was rejected as a reference - it carries two modified .nem files and a 551,288-byte s1built.bin); reference ROM built in-parcel, 524,288 B, md5 09dadb5071eb35050067a32462e39c5f, certified by the corpus's own chkbitperfect.lua as bit-perfect with REV01. THE 318: reproduced twice, identical after sorting, 9 files / 67 sites / ELEVEN causes, no unclassified remainder; 250 of 318 on seven source lines, two lines carrying 166 (float literals + INT(), and macro default parameter values). L2/L3 VERIFIED BY ME INDEPENDENTLY, different enumeration parameter than the agent's probes: s1disasm build.lua:28 passes p2bin `-p=FF -z=0,kosinski,Size_of_DAC_driver_guess,after` - so gap fill is FF where main.rs flattens with 0x00 (618 B), and p2bin Kosinski-compresses the DAC driver in-image post-assembly (5,983 B). THREE BRIEF CORRECTIONS, all ratified after firsthand checks: (1) my frontend/link dichotomy misses L3 entirely, which is at neither; (2) the 318 are the opposite of a long tail; (3) the 'diagnoses but proceeds' category I called the whole value of the ranking is EMPTY - sigil-frontend-as/src/lib.rs:30, Failure carries only diags+sources and the signature is Result<Module, Failure>, so no partial module survives and one diagnostic is as fatal as 318. TAGGED FOR FOREGROUND, not claimed: the stub ROM was never executed.

headline: A label written on the same line as a conditional now binds - and the real rule turned out to be four exceptions deep, none of which we would have guessed.
matters: Sonic 1 drops from 318 complaints to 305, exactly the thirteen predicted, and one whole class goes to zero. But the interesting part is what the obvious fix would have got wrong. 'Bind the label' is right for a line that OPENS a block, and the value is the position of that line whether the condition is true or false - same source, both settings, same answer. It is wrong everywhere else: a macro definition swallows its label and binds nothing, and a label on a line that CLOSES a block binds only if that arm actually ran. The agent got all of this by asking the reference assembler and reading its listings rather than reasoning, then proved it by deliberately breaking its own fix four ways and confirming each break was caught. A uniform fix would have invented four symbols that should not exist. On safety: this code sits in the engine's shipping build path, so it had to prove it moved no engine bytes - the construct appears zero times in the three files that route through it, and all four ROM shapes rebuilt byte-identical. I verified those four myself rather than taking the report.
detail: Landed at master b5c4f83f (merge of the label-on-directive-line fix, tip b1d80f07, 3 commits), pushed and verified by ls-remote. Eighteenth landing. eval.rs +99 (head_label/bind_head_label, called from the seven block-opener arms and from exec_if for the line terminating a taken arm); new test file label_on_directive_line.rs (9 tests); note 2026-09-04-as-label-on-if-line.md; gap-ledger row closed. ORACLE-DERIVED, asl listing rows quoted in the note: opener binds PC of its own line under both TRUE and FALSE; ifdef/ifndef/rept/irp/irpc/while/switch/case heads all bind; `L: macro` and `L: endm` bind NOTHING; a closer binds only on the arm that ran, mirrored on else, at most one per if-region; an if-line label opens the local scope. RED-FIRST, and the agent noticed the gap in its own proof: baseline gave 5 failed/4 passed, and the 4 passing are 'binds nothing' shapes that fix-first cannot speak for - so it mutated the LANDED fix three times, each shown by git diff -U1 and restored from HEAD, taking all four red. SUITE 379 suites 4375/0/2 CARGO_EXIT 0; taken on report rather than re-run to avoid contending with the relayout refreeze on the critical path - disclosed rather than implied. AEON IDENTITY VERIFIED BY ME: .aeon-as-fold at 4f5ad5a1, s4 14ee2440/719700, s4.debug 142294b3/737683, demo 0c456778/96474, demo.debug 2e603d53/101339, all identical to golden. THE BRIEF WAS WRONG THREE WAYS and the agent refused to reconcile: (1) the naive uniform fix would over-bind in four places; (2) my '16 link failures' claim is NOT verified by this parcel and must not be read as closed - S1 still exits 1 on the other 305 so link never runs; (3) my 'reproduction already committed, do not duplicate' was half wrong - one of the two lives outside the repo. LEFT OPEN: case/elsecase/endcase closers (our switch is string-only, refuses AS's integer form); a macro-expansion-local label we bind globally; an indented colon-less directive head asl refuses outright.

headline: The assembler can no longer claim a clean tree over a binary built from uncommitted code.
matters: Our version banner prints a clean-or-dirty word, and the engine's strict build gate trusts it. The word could say clean while the binary had just been rebuilt around an uncommitted edit - so the one gate that exists to catch a binary built from unsaved work would wave it through. It now tracks the actual source files the program is built from, so an unsaved edit turns the word to dirty. A second, smaller fault on the same instrument: it printed a recipe for checking itself that silently returns nothing in the shell this machine actually uses, which reads like a clean answer.

headline: The assembler can do decimal numbers now - and 330 bytes of the real Sonic 1 cartridge come out of it exactly right for the first time.
matters: Those two sound-frequency tables were the only remaining gap that owned actual cartridge bytes, so this is the first piece of Sonic 1 we can prove correct against the retail game rather than against our own expectations. The difference map against the real cartridge went from seven regions down to five. It also turned up a real bug in code we already ship: we were treating a division of two whole numbers as decimal, which the real assembler does not, and that produces silently wrong bytes rather than a complaint. Sonic 1's remaining errors are down to 93 from 259 this morning.
detail: master c041f238 (pushed, ls-remote verified), merge of parcel/as-float-int (tip 803ec63d, ancestor of master - landing proved). FM_Notes $072790 192B and PSGFrequencies $0729CE 138B: differing=0 against a retail REV01 ROM re-derived in a pristine worktree (chkbitperfect certifies it). Divergence map 7 regions/7285B -> 5/7003B. Design call: typed evaluator (Num=Int|Float) rather than a chosen float precision, asl-FORCED not preferred - INT(-7/2) is -3 because two ints make integer division and INT then floors an int; the old eval_float promoted to f64 on sight and answered -4. Verified independently by the overseer against asl: -3, plus INT(-3.2)=-4, INT(-3.0)=-3, INT(1e17+1-1e17)=0 pinning binary64 over 80-bit extended. Second cause, plainer: builtins were wired into dc.b alone; all four widths now share expand_operand_builtins. Floats stay front-end-only, 7.4 invariant intact. S1 259->93, S2 9432->9266, one class moving, none rising; diagnostic sets 0 new both corpora; unresolved-symbol name sets 0/0 both directions. Landing run on MERGED tree: 4409/0/2, 382 suites, 0 skip, 0 ratchet, CARGO_EXIT 0, tree clean, parcel test present in its own log. Aeon four shapes byte-identical and equal to the frozen goldens. 5 mutations each shown applied and red; M2 was green-on-applied and was treated as a runner defect, root-caused to two routes reaching an integer, closed with a no-float-token test, and M1 re-established under the strengthened suite (the retroactive-method clause firing). Agent refuted the brief on 4 points including one of its own predictions.

headline: Three tools were picking their own build directory, and one of them had already picked a different lane's compiler.
matters: Several of our scripts, when nobody told them where to build, reached into one folder shared by every copy of the project on this machine. That is not untidiness: the build cache cannot tell which copy an artifact came from, so a run can silently use a program compiled from somebody else's working copy - and one of the shared folders on this machine was holding exactly that, a compiler reporting a branch that had been deleted hours earlier. Two of the affected scripts are the ones that record what the correct output looks like, where a wrong compiler produces a complete, plausible, wrong record rather than an error. They now stop and say what they need. Separately, the message that warns when the compiler is older than the code now says WHICH version it compared against and whether that version is anything anyone else can see - the engine lane read that warning this morning and could not tell.
detail: sigil fix/shared-target-defaults-and-banner at 601bd63b, off master 1d5b00c2. The anchor is NAMED, not MOVED: re-anchoring the refusal at the remote would refuse every lane with unpushed commits, which is always-red. Measured before touching anything: .sigil-ref-target/release/sigil reported revision c9a81d7e, branch parcel/as-macro-default-params (deleted), source /home/volence/sonic_hacks/.sigil-f4. Red-first, seven mutations each shown on disk and restored from the committed baseline: the shared ref-target default (3 rows red, and it refuted my own prediction of 5 - the two REF_TARGET rows do not discriminate it), capture_goldens' fallback (2), derive's fallback (2), refreeze telling its child nothing (1), the unnamed anchor in both verdicts (2), an asserted-rather-than-measured published line (1), the published drift check re-anchored at HEAD (1). Landing run at 601bd63b against .aeon-f4ref@4f5ad5a1 (all four shapes present): 4429 passed / 0 failed / 2 ignored, 384 suites, 0 skip lines, CARGO_EXIT 0, GREEN; 4381 baseline + 48 new. headline: Nothing in the suite can now quietly pick up the wrong assembler - including the two scripts that write down what the game's bytes are supposed to be.
matters: That second part is the one that would have hurt. Those two scripts record the expected bytes everything else is checked against; with one setting unset they reached into a shared folder any lane might have overwritten, and a wrong assembler there would not have complained - it would have been written into the expectations under the wrong name, and every later check would have passed against a record of a build nobody made. They now refuse rather than guess.

Measured first: nothing depended on the retired default. refreeze DID rely on the fallback - fixed by DERIVATION (its own executable sits in the target dir) rather than a new required variable, since a refuse-by-default landing on a 3am freeze is a shape this lane retracted once. headline: Catching the shared assembler up to date will not change a single byte of the game - measured where it had never actually been measured.
matters: Several lanes build with an assembler months behind, and the gap touches the code that decides where things land in the cartridge. Three earlier checks said no movement, but all three tested the same frozen snapshot, so they were one check run three times. This tested it at the engine's real current state and the answer holds: all four builds identical, byte for byte. The rebuild is now a non-event that can be scheduled rather than a risk anyone has to absorb.
detail: master 655af4eb, merge of measure/assembler-drift-at-aeon-09d964c7 (tip e5bf4b79, docs-only). Four shapes identical between sigil 0a58f2ec and c041f238 at aeon 09d964c7 (a pinned SHA; their tree moved twice mid-run), cmp -l zero differing each. Second observation not a third repeat: subject differs from tip goldens by 465092/508867/28307/62475 bytes. Held fixed: tree, shape set, build order, NO_LINT, SIGIL_EMIT (one emitter both arms - build.sh:399 re-runs it per invocation so it is a live input; empirically free, two different emitter artifacts produce byte-identical output across all 19 sound artifacts). Separation control: aeon's OWN build log names the assembler per arm; arm A rebuilt after B and reproduced exactly, closing order effects. TWO FINDINGS OUTRANK THE NUMBER: the comparator passed its own non-vacuity proof for the WRONG REASON on first run (argv bug printed ABSENT for every case incl. the two meant to fail), fixed before anything trusted it; and a dead earlier run left four ROMs present, non-empty, plausibly sized that were frozen-tip goldens copied in during provisioning and never built - the mtime-post-dates-build assertion discriminated. A missing file announces itself; a wrong file corroborates itself. Aeon banked the twin (0a6dae9e) and checked their own exposure: their script rm -f's before building so existence proves freshness by construction, and they wrote down WHY the rm is there, which it was not before.

headline: Three directives for declaring runs of constants now work - and behind them were 3,200 complaints in Sonic 2 that had nothing to do with directives.
matters: Sonic 2 fell from 9,266 complaints to 6,035, its biggest single drop. Three lines in one file build the whole vocabulary the game uses to name parts of an object in memory; hundreds of readable names are built on those, and thousands of instructions use those names. None of it could resolve. The stronger evidence than the count: 190 names started resolving and not one name stopped, checked in both directions - a count alone cannot tell those apart.
detail: master 5450b2bc (pushed, ls-remote verified; agent tip 68714776 an ancestor). S1 93->65 exactly the 28 predicted, no class risen, none new. S2 9266->6035; unresolved-symbol-in-operand 3384->184; 190 names left the unresolved set, 0 entered. Semantics asl-minted, 20 rows; two would be got wrong by a plausible reading (the step is read at the moment a member advances the counter and never applied retroactively; an explicit member moves the counter, which is what makes the corpus's enharmonic note aliases work). Six red-first mutations each shown applied and restored; all 13 tests red under at least one. Four aeon shapes byte-identical, built twice from two toolchains. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 4442/0/2, 385 suites, 0 skip, 0 ratchet, clean tree, GREEN. THE AGENT REFUTED THE BRIEF'S CENTRAL MECHANISM: the dc.b deferral is real but not enum-specific, and instruction operands DO resolve in the front end, so S2's 3,200 were already loud and merely misattributed - 'makes names measurable for the first time' holds for S1 and is wrong for S2. TWO SELF-INFLICTED ERRORS TODAY, both mine and both caught by gates: my standing-artifact declaration took the boot doc over its byte bound and turned master red (repaired by moving closed history out, losslessness proven both directions); and I committed the d-25 card while this landing run was in flight, invalidating it, which is the exact failure my own boot doc warns of and which I had written into this agent's own brief an hour earlier. Cost: one full re-run.

headline: The document I read at the start of every session had grown past its size limit - because of an edit I made this morning - and repairing it turned up two places where it contradicted itself.
matters: That file is the first thing any session reads, so a contradiction in it is inherited by whoever boots next. One of the two was a rule stated twice with the WRONG version first: it asserted an exactness that the second version explicitly corrects as only an approximation. A cold reader would take the first and stop. The size limit itself has a gate, which caught this within hours rather than letting the file drift.
detail: Repaired at 48e5e4d5 after my own standing-artifact declaration (1078a076) took docs/OVERSEER.md from 99,835 to 100,690 bytes against a 100,000 bound, turning master red; found by the enum agent, which reported it rather than absorbing it. Fixed by moving closed history to OVERSEER-LOG.md, not by shaving a ruling (the owner's cut ruling forbids the latter): the 'NEXT PARCEL - case folding' block described work landed at 849a2412, verified an ancestor of master before being called closed, and was actively misdirecting a cold boot; the empty-commit-range episode moved whole with its rule kept as a pointer to protocol bar 16(a). Losslessness proven both directions - every non-blank moved line found verbatim in the log. Two contradictions repaired that saved no bytes: the suite-reconcile instruction appeared twice and DISAGREED, the refuted identity version first; and a paragraph duplicating protocol text became a pointer only after a line-oriented grep first said it was NOT duplicated - the prose is wrapped, so that check silently reports absent for text that is present, and acting on it would have deleted local text while reporting compliance. This closed AS-SECTION-STALE-STATUS as a side effect; both it and AS-ENUM-DIRECTIVE are now dropped from the queue rather than marked done, which is not a state the board accepts.

headline: Two more places the assembler quietly did the wrong thing are closed - and the agents corrected me on what the problems actually were in both cases.
matters: One was real and ugly: a mis-ordered argument list was being assembled into a DIFFERENT ROM with no complaint and a success code. The other turned out not to be the bug we had written down - the check already exists and already refuses, just not on the path a single file takes, so it was left open with the reasoning rather than 'fixed' by breaking the part that was right. A third problem neither row mentioned is worse than both and is now written down: a case where our assembler and the reference BOTH succeed and produce different bytes.
detail: master 71d8373e (pushed). Layout: f8b7fdc9, 4453/0/2, 385 suites, GREEN. Silent-acceptance: 71d8373e, 4461/0/2, 386 suites, GREEN, parcel test named in its own log. Four aeon shapes byte-identical on both. LAYOUT REFUTED THE BRIEF THREE WAYS: align emits no image bytes at all in asl (the .p has no record for skipped addresses, so p2bin's fill decides them - same object gives 11 00 22 under -p=0x0 and 11 ff 22 under -p=0xFF, and the old code comment claimed asl verification for a byte asl never writes); it was 1 and 3 extra bytes, not two; and the odd-address rule is two defects, neither about lone labels - ds pads to the next EVEN address regardless of width and fires with no label, and exactly ONE label absorbs a pad, the most recently defined, so two labels at one place hold different values, already reachable through dc.w before this parcel touched ds. 33/33 probes byte-identical to asl including symbol addresses. Reachability nil and stated as such: both disassemblies shadow the builtin align with a macro, both set padding off before their first byte, no odd-address ds in either corpus by parity walk. SILENT-ACCEPTANCE: row 2 confirmed and fixed (#1811 implemented alongside #1812 - one recognition site, so scoping to the named one would have left the neighbour silently accepted); row 1 REFUTED, the linker already refuses but only on the resolve_layout path, a seam not a missing check; the #320 divergence ledgered with a kill condition rather than patched. Population newly refused EMPTY, measured by census across both disassemblies and all four aeon shapes. BOTH AGENTS DEPARTED FROM CONTRADICTORY BRIEFS I WROTE: the layout one on the anchor, the silent one because a landing run WRITES into the aeon tree it was told not to write to, so it provisioned its own at the same revision and proved it with repin --check. Second time today I handed an agent two incompatible instructions.

headline: Your ROM re-layout is in - the sound banks moved up the cartridge and the engine has its 98,304 bytes a shape of room back.
matters: This is the thing you said yes to this morning. It is reversible with one edit and a rebuild if you ever want the space back. Two things worth knowing: it only works paired with a matching change on the engine side, which lands next and cannot build until this one did - and I twice had the order of that pairing backwards. Nothing was landed on the wrong story, because an agent checked the premise before implementing rather than after.

Banks at 0xA8000/0xB8000; pins.rs:277 DAC_BANKS plain_base 0xA8000 verified at the source, not asserted from a grep that had returned nothing. Assembler relinked to 756c7efd, md5 58db359428e9b38e633836313bf40487; aeon re-pinned. THE PREMISE I HAD WRONG TWICE: I told two lanes the parked freeze named an abandoned line of aeon history and had expired. It names aeon's own pushed branch parcel/rom-relayout-more-room - their unlanded half of this same parcel - so the freeze never expired and re-taking it elsewhere is impossible, not inadvisable: the bank addresses are compiled into the assembler, so aeon master's tree refuses by name. Proved by A/B with the assembler as the only variable, then confirmed from the other end when aeon's merged tree died on the mirror lint at 0x90000 - a prediction I put in writing before their build returned. An absence from aeon master meant NOT YET LANDED and I read it as WALKED AWAY FROM. Also booked: our own rev_reachability called 5875e60e PERMANENTLY orphaned; it asks only origin/master, and the revision is reachable from the pushed branch. Third self-contradictory brief of the day (never degrade the freeze vs the pairing gate must pass against your tree); the agent obeyed the right half and said so.

headline: Your re-layout is fully in - and the engine lane's own checksums for it do not reproduce here, which I have flagged before anything else lands on them.
matters: The record of what the game's bytes are is now anchored to the engine's real master rather than a side branch, which was the last piece. But when I rebuilt the game in a clean copy of that exact revision, I got four different checksums from the ones the engine lane reported. I ruled out the assembler by experiment - their own pinned copy of it, in my clean tree, agrees with me. Their machine was building with uncommitted changes at the time, which explains part of it and NOT all of it, so I have said so rather than offering the tidy half. They rebuild in a clean copy before anything stacks on top.

Chain entry #203 relayout-at-aeon-master, aeon_rev 483b3e128ec4b9efc77a9d2e8a8c7679e961cea8, refreeze --check OK at len 203. AEON'S FOUR reproduce none of them; control build with their own pinned binary (md5 58db3594, rev 756c7efd) in the same clean tree gives my figures, so the assembler is excluded by experiment. FOURTH self-contradictory brief of the day, flagged by the agent rather than silently resolved.

headline: CORRECTION: there was no divergence. The engine's build and mine were byte-identical all along - we were comparing two different kinds of checksum.
matters: My previous entry told you four checksums did not reproduce and the cause was unresolved. That was wrong. Their number and mine were the SAME FILE measured two different ways, and both are eight hex digits, so four of one lined up against four of the other read as four mismatches rather than as a category error. Nothing needs re-doing, nothing was ever wrong, and the frozen record describes exactly the build they produced. Correcting it here because the earlier entry is in front of you and is false.
detail: Verified on my own artifact rather than accepted from the relay: /home/volence/sonic_hacks/.aeon-ref-relayout-master/s4.bin gives md5 31813fd8069d80100410cac374bdced7 and crc32 1c09fbfc at size 819131 - so aeon's reported '31813fd8' is the md5 prefix of the very file whose crc32 is '1c09fbfc'. All four pairs match. Their clean rebuild also reproduced their original figures, so the dirty-tree hypothesis was wrong too. WHAT MADE IT CONVINCING: a truncated md5 and a crc32 are both eight hex digits, so a unit mismatch produced well-formed values of exactly the right shape and did not announce itself. Both lanes then reasoned PAST it rather than AT it - I built a control with the shared pinned binary, checked closure revisions and frozen tables, and inspected their working tree, all sound and all aimed at explaining a difference that did not exist; they found a size discriminator and read it as pointing at their own side when the sizes had agreed all along. Neither of us asked what FUNCTION the other's number came from, which was the only question that mattered. Aeon now labels every checksum with its function name and size. Chain #203 stands unchanged and correct; the vertical band is unparked.

headline: The assembler now stops where the source tells it to stop - and two things we had written down as bugs turned out not to be bugs at all.
matters: The real fault was that a source file can say 'stop assembling here' and we kept reading past it, quietly adding bytes nobody asked for. The other two entries on my list claimed the old assembler accepted something we refused. It does not - it refuses exactly what we refuse, and one of the two descriptions was simply backwards. Both of those had been marked closed earlier on the strength of a complaint count falling to zero, which is the measurement that cannot tell 'correct' apart from 'quietly accepts anything'. They are now held down by actual bytes taken from the real assembler, so they cannot drift back without something going red. Your game's bytes did not move: all four builds were rebuilt and came out identical.
detail: Branch parcel/as-silent-divergences merged at 8e41a78b, pushed on master 0cf84bcf. AS-END-DIRECTIVE fixed in sigil-frontend-as eval.rs ('end' now sets the existing quiet stop-the-pass flag); AS-WORD-IMM-RAM-LABEL refuted (asl refuses the shape too - both accept exactly -32768..=65535) and AS-CNOP-ORG-CONST refuted (assembles clean); both re-pinned with asl-minted golden byte blocks plus as_word_immediate_range.rs. Oracle was the committed asl 1.42 Beta Bld 212 in the corpus repos. Regenerating the whole golden file reproduced all 201 pre-existing blocks byte-identically, re-proving non-circularity. Suite on the merged tree: 388 suites, 4468 passed / 1 failed, the single failure being the boot-doc size ratchet tripped by my own docs edit, not the parcel; re-run green after rewriting that edit shorter. aeon shapes rebuilt in .aeon-verify-483, all four CRC32+size identical to the frozen goldens. Reviewed here before landing: every consumer of the 'aborted' flag enumerated (pure control flow, mapped to no error result).

headline: Our nightly safety net could report a name as missing when it was actually present - and it only did it when the machine was busy.
matters: This is the more serious of today's two findings and we found it by accident. The nightly job that checks the engine's source asks 'is this file on my list' in a way that, under load, reads a MATCH as a NON-match. When it trips, the whole nightly backstop refuses to run - dark, reporting nothing - and it also turns an unrelated piece of work red, so the failure looks like it belongs to whoever was unlucky enough to be running at the time. It can only ever fail in that one direction. It survived because running the check on its own can never reproduce it: you have to run it inside a busy machine. Fixed at the one site. I reproduced it independently before accepting it - 9 failures in 9,600 runs under load, none at all in 400 run one at a time.
detail: scripts/nightly_source_gates.sh: membership was `printf '%s\n' "${SOURCE_GATES[@]}" | grep -qx "$n"` under the file's own `set -o pipefail`. grep -q exits on match, printf takes SIGPIPE, pipefail returns 141, so the if takes the else branch on a match. Replaced with a pure-bash loop. Agent measured 8 wrong classifications in 192 concurrent audits and 25/9,600 on the isolated pipeline, every one status 141, 0/4,000 serial. Independently reproduced here over a synthetic list: 9/9600 concurrent all status 141, 0/400 serial. Script uses set -uo pipefail (no -e), so the loop's non-zero exit on a no-match is harmless; verified. Class not yet swept - same construct elsewhere would have the same fault, booked as SOURCE-GATE-PIPEFAIL-CLASSES.

headline: Our end-of-run check now runs the code-style check itself - and the reason it had to is that the check had been failing on master all day without anyone seeing it.
matters: The bar we say we hold has always included the linter. The wrapper never ran it, so meeting that bar depended on a person running it by hand - and the obvious hand command PRINTS every complaint and still exits successfully. So the loudest possible evidence was sitting on screen while the exit code said fine. It is now inside the wrapper, its exit code sits next to the test result, and a red linter makes the run not-green exactly like a failing test, with no way to skip it. The complaints themselves were tabs inside listings copied verbatim from the reference assembler - the tabs are that assembler's own column separators, so they are evidence and not untidiness. headline: The assembler now refuses to let a name change its kind - and the thing we had written down was half the problem.
matters: A name in assembly is either a fixed constant or a variable you can reassign. The real assembler refuses to let one become the other, in EITHER direction, and we allowed both. The sharpest case: on three lines where the reference assembler stops with two errors and produces no file at all, we produced a file with DIFFERENT BYTES and said nothing. Two assemblers, one source, two different cartridges, and no complaint to tell you. Our note described only one of the two directions, so half of it was never written down anywhere. Both are closed now. Your game is unaffected: all four builds come out byte-for-byte identical, and both reference disassemblies produce identical output, so nothing in any real source does the thing we now refuse.

headline: CORRECTION to my last entry: I cited the wrong commit for the tool fix, and I did it by skipping the exact check I had just told two other lanes to run.
matters: The finding itself is unchanged - the tool was wrong, our document was fine, and the fixed tool still catches a real tear. What was wrong is the commit I named as carrying the fix. Twice tonight I corrected other people for citing a commit that merely CONTAINS a change rather than the one that makes it. Then I did the same thing, and worse: I ran the file-list check on the commit I DOUBTED and not on the one I PROPOSED. The evidence was on my own screen - I printed the file list, saw one test file and no tool file, and read the commit's TITLE instead. A title is a claim about a change; the file list is the change. There is nothing to re-verify in the result, and nothing dangling now.

headline: The build's per-game values now reach the listing - and the agent refuted a measurement I had written into our own rulebook.
matters: Values your build sets per game - how many rings the ring buffer holds, 128 in one game and 16 in the other - appeared in the debugger listing nowhere at all, while constants written in source did. So a debugger panel could not show a capacity ceiling without hardcoding a number that is wrong for one game by construction. They are there now, and your game's bytes did not move - and this time that is guaranteed by how the code is built rather than by my having measured it once. THE PART WORTH YOUR ATTENTION IS MY MISTAKE: I had written into our rulebook that the debug build always carries exactly one more of these than the release build, and prescribed a check based on it. The agent measured the second game: identical, 555 and 555. My figure came from four looks at ONE game, written down as a fact about both. A check built to my sentence would have failed on the demo game from the day it was written, on perfectly correct code - which is precisely the trap that same page warns about. The rule survives; the number I attached to it does not, and I have struck it rather than quietly softening it.
detail: master 835884cf, then the doc correction. Listing-only by design, argued as BETTER than full symbols: a link symbol adds nothing a .lst reader consumes, would make a bare MAX_RING_BUFFER RESOLVE in an operand where it is a loud unresolved-symbol error today (a silent language-surface change with no consumer), and has no counterpart to the seeded-define precedence rule. Byte-neutrality is STRUCTURAL: append_deb2_appendix filters is_equate at the deb2 boundary (native.rs:4480, verified here), and the appendix is the only listing consumer that becomes ROM bytes - so it is a property, not a repeated measurement. headline: Two more directives implemented - but the find of the night is a number our assembler writes in decimal where the real one writes it in hex, and it reaches the cartridge.
matters: The parcel itself is small and safe: two directives that used to be hard errors now work, so sources that were refused will assemble, and nothing that already built can change. WHAT MATTERS IS WHAT IT TRIPPED OVER. When source text embeds a computed number into a string, the real assembler writes that number in HEX and we write it in DECIMAL. With the value 42 the real assembler puts '2A' in the cartridge and we put '42' - different bytes, no complaint from either side. It has been invisible because every test anyone ever wrote for that feature used a single-digit number, where hex and decimal are the same characters. So the feature had a proof that could not fail. Nothing in your game uses it today, and the agent deliberately did NOT fix it inside a parcel whose whole safety claim was that it could not move bytes. It is written down with what closing it needs.
detail: master e738f965. warning/exitm implemented against asl 1.42; both were hard errors under BOTH processors before, so the no-byte-change property is structural. exitm ends the INNERMOST EXPANSION (a bare top-level rept counts, with no macro anywhere) - my brief said 'current macro invocation' and was wrong, as is asl's own message. asl SEGFAULTS on exitm inside irp/irpc (exit 139, both nestings) so that cell has no oracle; sigil takes the sibling-consistent reading and ships the test LABELLED COVERAGE, NOT A GATE. 13 asl-minted byte vectors + 10 diagnostic gates; 8 mutations each shown applied and each red, and the runner ABORTED on one that failed to apply rather than reporting a pass. Interpolation finding verified by me firsthand: asl binds n:=42 as the string '2A' (bytes 32 41); sigil's own doc comments at eval.rs:1727/:1742 say it folds to decimal. Reaches bytes via str_env -> dc.b. Ledgered with kill condition (needs asl probes for negative values and function returns, plus a four-shape CRC re-proof) because the fix is byte-changing and moves error/fatal/message with it. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 391 suites (independently counted), 4500/0/2, 0 skip, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, GREEN, reconciles 4490+10. Four shapes CRC32+size unchanged.

headline: A name that means two things at once was being read as the wrong one - and the booked description of the problem was wrong about what it even was.
matters: In the Sonic 2 disassembly the name 'id' is used for two different things: an offset into an object's record, and a lookup function. Our assembler saw 'id(a1)' and read it as a call to the function, substituting a CPU register into it. The reference assembler peels the addressing mode off first and never has the ambiguity. Mostly this produced refusals - 274 complaints now gone, with no new ones anywhere. But it could also produce a WRONG INSTRUCTION SILENTLY: where the reference writes to an offset from a register, we wrote to a fixed address instead. Same length, clean exit, no complaint. That is the second such case tonight. Our note called this 'one arm of a macro wrapper'; it is neither an arm nor about that wrapper, and 115 of the 274 are at ordinary instructions the note never mentioned. Your game is untouched and that is checked twice over: its files never define one of these functions, so the confusion cannot arise, and the seven places that DO have the risky shape rebuild to identical bytes.
detail: master 352578a0. Cause was one line in Evaluator::lower_m68k running expand_calls over the whole operand token list before parse_operands; fixed with a narrowing peel (m68k_ea_base_spans + expand_calls_m68k_operands) that can only reduce the expansion window and only for an operand ending in a register base group. Refuted an in-repo comment that asserted whole-operand expansion was safe because register-indirect EAs pass through untouched - true only while no function name abuts the paren, and it was the reason nobody looked. Corpus 6035 -> 5761 (-274), zero new diagnostics either direction; booked sites 159 of them, the other 115 at plain move.b/cmpi.b/tst.b/cmp.b. Six gates, two mutations each shown applied, and the two failure directions separated (neither mutation leaves all gates green or all red). Four shapes CRC32+size unchanged, rebuilt with the HEAD-baked binary. Aeon safety verified here with a positive control: no AS 'function' defined in its three .asm files (the word appears only in comments), and 7 name(reg) sites exist so the byte proof is not vacuous. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 392 suites (independently counted), 4504/0/2, 0 skip, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, GREEN.

headline: The risky one is in and it broke nothing - because the survey found that my own description of the danger was wrong before anyone wrote code.
matters: This is the parcel I held overnight because it makes the assembler REFUSE more, and refusing more is how a build stops. I told the agent the population was 'every duplicated label and every twice-included header'. That was wrong, and taking it literally would have shipped an assembler that refuses 97 places in the Sonic 2 disassembly which the real one accepts happily. Labels written inside a repeated or macro-expanded block are LOCAL in the real assembler - they never become real names at all - so they are not part of the rule. That was 97 of the 97 cases the survey found. The survey ran first, which is the only reason the risk never arrived. Your four builds are unchanged, all seven shapes still build, and both reference disassemblies produce identical output. There was nothing to hand back to the engine lane. AND IT FOUND SOMETHING BIGGER ON THE WAY: if a source file includes the same header twice, the real assembler includes it TWICE and we include it ONCE - different cartridge contents, and neither tool says a word. I checked that myself both ways. Not touched; it is written down.
detail: master b3ebb160. Census enumerated with the COMPILER not grep (colliding names come from macro expansion, \{} interpolation and scope qualification and do not exist in source text): each tree assembled with branch-point and new binaries, diagnostic streams diffed - aeon 4 shapes CRC32+size unchanged, 7 shipped shapes strict-green, s1disasm 57 diff-empty, s2disasm 5761 diff-empty. Positive control: duplicated equ injected with EQUAL values, shown on disk, red by name; unmutated tree green. The un-narrowed rule refused 97 s2 sites (start x36, end x3, __LABEL__Plc x58). Narrowing records NOTHING for expansion-local forms rather than recording-and-not-refusing - recording would make a later file-level equ a redefinition of a symbol asl says does not exist (mutation M3, red). 11 gates, 4 mutations each shown applied and restored, red at 3/1/1/4. 16 probes x 3 runs = one hash, so the reference assembler's known non-determinism touched nothing. headline: The hex-versus-decimal bug is fixed - and the agent proved its own best evidence did not prove what it looked like it proved.
matters: An embedded number now renders the way the real assembler renders it. Your four builds are byte-identical. But the agent did something I want to point at: it tested whether that byte-identity actually MEANT anything, by breaking the new code so hard it would crash if it ever ran - and all four builds still came out perfect. So your game never uses this feature at all, and the identical bytes prove that nothing ELSE moved, not that this change is safe where it is used. It said so plainly instead of banking a clean result. I checked and it is right: there are exactly two places in your engine that use it, both inside error messages that only fire when something has already gone wrong. It also found the cell that decided the whole fix, which nobody had written down: the same assembler uses HEX when building a string and DECIMAL when building a NAME. A reasonable-looking version of this fix would have passed every test and quietly broken the Sonic 2 disassembly's zone table at zone 10.
detail: master bea42871. One line: interp_text calls a new render_interp_int (format {:X} over u64), which moves warning/error/fatal/message, both string-binding branches of directive_equate/directive_set, and eval_name_brace's STRING arm; its integer arm stays decimal deliberately and its doc now says why. Probes r1-r13 committed, each run three times: negative renders 64-bit two's complement (-1 -> FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF), function returns render like any integer, zero is one digit. asl's non-determinism touched nothing here. NON-VACUITY CONTROL: render_interp_int replaced by panic!, all four shapes still built at identical CRCs - so the four-shape identity attests nothing else in eval.rs moved, NOT that this change is exercised; corroborated independently here (aeon has exactly 2 interpolation sites, both in error directives on failure paths). Eight values render differently so zone_id_10..17 became zone_id_A..11, invisible because both sides share the renderer. The two stale asl-verified comments RE-VERIFIED with a distinguishing value; the old claim was true and could not have been false. headline: A label inside a macro now belongs to that copy of the macro - and the danger I warned about pointed the wrong way entirely.
matters: I briefed this as risky because it would stop names resolving, and a stopped build is the worst outcome. That was backwards. The measurement showed our assembler was already REFUSING eight of the nine basic shapes the real one accepts happily: a macro used twice defined the same label twice and our linker rejected it. Doing what I asked for would have added MORE refusals and fixed none of them. The real rule is that each use of a macro, and each turn of a loop, owns its own labels. That removes the refusals instead of adding to them. Your four builds are unchanged - though honestly, none of your code uses this at all, and the agent said so rather than letting four identical builds look like a safety proof.
detail: master ceb5cdf0. Per-instance label namespaces chained inward-to-outward (scan_plain_labels, ExpansionLabelScope, push/pop_expansion_labels, plain_label_scope, sym_key, resolve_sym, define_label, directive_include, wired at qualify_expr + four bare-identifier resolve sites). Corpus diffs empty both ways AND non-vacuous, since 361 instances engage. Not reached in aeon (instances-with-labels=0 every pass every shape) and the refusal path is unreachable there by construction - a PC label in the residual root trips [layout.undeclared-alignment] first, proven by injection. 11 fixtures, 5 mutations; M5 applied and stayed GREEN first time, reported as a runner defect, a new asl-measured probe added, M5 red on it now. headline: A method correction that reaches back over tonight: our check for whether the reference assembler answers consistently was partly measuring its own stopwatch.
matters: Several times tonight I recorded that we had confirmed the reference assembler gives a stable answer by running a probe three times and comparing. Its output includes how long it took to run, which is a number that can change between runs. So that comparison was partly checking a clock. THE DIRECTION IS THE SAVING GRACE AND I WANT TO BE PRECISE RATHER THAN DRAMATIC: if the three runs came out IDENTICAL - which is what happened every time - then the content matched too, so every 'stable' verdict I banked still holds. What the flaw can do is raise a FALSE ALARM, telling us the assembler disagreed with itself when only the clock moved. Nobody has been misled; the check needs the timing line removed before anyone trusts it reporting a DIFFERENCE.
detail: Found by the macro-label agent, verified here: every asl listing carries an 'N.NN seconds assembly time' line, and being a duration it can straddle a tick. On a trivial probe it is stably 0.00 (10/10 runs identical here), which is why it hid. The #1000 parcel's sixteen-probe stability table used the same pipeline. Formally: identical-hash implies identical-content, so the false-PASS direction is closed and no banked conclusion is withdrawn; only the false-ALARM direction is open. Booked as ORACLE-STABILITY-CHECK-TIMER to strip the line before hashing.

headline: We were silently accepting programs that assemble forever - the guard I thought was protecting us was hiding them.
matters: Including the same file twice now works the way the real assembler works. But the real finding is the opposite of what I expected. I had assumed our guard against runaway inclusion was a safety feature, and warned the agent that removing it might make the assembler hang. It was the reverse: a file that includes ITSELF, and a pair of files that include each other, are broken programs the real assembler stops on - and ours assembled them CLEAN, no complaint, and wrote a cartridge. The guard was not protecting us from the runaway case; it was hiding it. The real assembler has no cycle detection at all, just a depth limit of 199, which I verified myself. We now match it. Your builds are unchanged, and only two files in your whole engine use include at all - so those identical bytes prove the plumbing is intact and nothing about the new behaviour, which the agent proved rather than claimed.
detail: master 634a520c. visited: BTreeSet<PathBuf> -> include_depth bounded at INCLUDE_NEST_MAX=199 with asl's own message, refusal setting aborted to match its fatal. asl measured: 199 copies then error #10008 (verified here firsthand), depth not repetition (199 distinct pass / 200 refuse / 250 sequential clean), nestmax does not govern it, diamond assembles twice, path spelling never compared. Engagement counter: aeon executed=1 repeats=0 across 48 passes, s1 439/439 repeats=0, s2 339 seen/300 executed repeats=0. Controls: panic! at top of directive_include FAILS all four shapes (plumbing reached); panic! on the repeat path BUILDS all four (population zero); duplicating aeon's one include line makes the OLD binary emit a byte-identical ROM while the new one refuses by name. SIX mutations, and THREE OF SIX first landed green - incl. the class worth naming: fixtures that derived their chains FROM INCLUDE_NEST_MAX could not disagree with it. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 395 suites (independently counted), 4538/0/2, 0 skip, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, GREEN, reconciling 4528+10.

headline: Fixed the way I was checking the reference assembler answers consistently - and it turned out I was ignoring the wrong clock.
matters: Our check ran a test three times and compared the output, to confirm the old assembler gives the same answer twice. Its output carries a timestamp, so part of what we were comparing was a clock. I dispatched this to strip the one clock I knew about. The agent found a SECOND one I had missed, and it is worse: the banner carries the time of day INCLUDING 'AM' or 'PM', and the old filter removed the time but left the AM/PM. So any batch of runs straddling noon or midnight would report the assembler contradicting itself - guaranteed twice a day, where the one I knew about was occasional. It also proved the fixed filter still catches a genuine difference, which was the real risk: a filter that removes too much turns the check into one that passes everything. Nothing in your game is affected; this is entirely about how we measure.
detail: master 11295e94 + the doc corrections at 3542666b. Population was ONE runner, not the several I briefed - everything else in the tree compares bytes or hashes a binary; the interesting finding is a runner that should exist and did not. Shared declock.sed with a 14-case selfcheck and a 5-mutation runner; the gate that matters is two listings with identical clocks and ONE emitted byte different still diffing. Mutations include an over-strip and a sink filter, both red. One mutation came back applied-and-still-green and was diagnosed correctly as a mis-built instrument (perl ate $RANDOM so the patch added a CONSTANT, and a constant is not instability) rather than booked as a pass. The agent also made the timer vary DETERMINISTICALLY by scaling asl's workload - 0.00 to 3 minutes across four orders of magnitude - which exposed a 'N minute, N.NN seconds' form my stated spelling missed and the existing anchor did not match; I had predicted this could only be reasoned about. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 395 suites (independently counted), 4538/0/2, 0 skip, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, GREEN, no ROM touched.

headline: And I corrected two of my own records that this invalidated - one of which was never checkable in the first place.
matters: Twice tonight I wrote down that we had confirmed the reference assembler was consistent, quoting a hash. One of those notes never said WHICH command produced the hash - so nobody can re-run it, and three reasonable interpretations all give different numbers. That claim is not wrong; it is UNCHECKABLE, which is worse in a quiet way, because on the page it looks exactly like a verified one. The other note's numbers were real but no longer reproduce, because fixing the clock filter moves all of them. I kept both sets of numbers with the correction written beside them rather than quietly swapping them, so a reader can see they moved and why. The findings they supported are unchanged. What I got wrong earlier was saying 'nothing is withdrawn' - true of the conclusions, not of the evidence, and a number nobody can reproduce is indistinguishable from one nobody checked.

headline: The old assembler's unreliability turns out to belong to one COPY of it, not to the version - and four copies on this machine all claim to be the same.
matters: We check our assembler against an old one. That old one sometimes gives a different answer every time it runs, silently. I had this written down as a fault of 'version 1.42 Beta 212'. It is a fault of one particular COPY: there are four of these binaries on your machine, all printing that exact version string, and only ONE of them misbehaves. So the version string cannot tell you which you are holding - and I had been using the bad one for every check I made tonight. I went back and re-ran my two most important findings on BOTH copies, three times each: they agree and are steady, so nothing I told you is affected. The good news is bigger: our frozen byte-comparisons - the ones that would have been worthless if minted from a random value - were re-made using the BAD copy and came out identical, which proves none of them depends on it. That check does not rely on repetition, so it is much stronger than running things more times.
detail: master 71ab08d7. Builds: s2disasm asl md5 0dee1f98 VARIES, s1disasm 61e67256 stable, identical banners (verified here). Trigger is not the function/register/immediate as I had it: minimal form is an UNDEFINED symbol in an immediate, and the class is wider than symbols since range-refused immediates with no symbol vary too - any operand asl declined to value. Mechanism is an uninitialized read, collapsing to constant $5555 under setarch -R. The silent arm (#f(<reg>) with f defined) is exit 0 no diagnostic and is the only one that can reach a minting tool. Sweep: 193 probes x 100 runs uniform = 0 unstable; native-binary run found 2 (wimm/wrange in the as-end-probes dir, whose runner names the bad build); 20-run control against the bad build = 16 unstable, proving the sweep fires. THREE asl-minted golden corpora (not the one I briefed): snippets 223 blocks, m68k 176, z80 120 - all stable at N=40 AND cross-minted with the UNSTABLE build byte-identical, which is N-independent. My own re-check: interpolation 3241 and include-twice=2 copies, both builds, 3 runs each, agreeing. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 395 suites (independently counted), 4538/0/2, 0 skip, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, GREEN, no ROM moved.

headline: Our own boot instructions were telling every session to use the unreliable copy of the old assembler, by name.
matters: The document every session reads before starting work named a specific copy of the old assembler and said 'use it'. That is the one copy that answers differently every run. It has been saying so since Sept 3rd. Nothing we measured is wrong because of it - the work that used it happened to stay clear of the unreliable cases, and I re-checked my own two most important findings against BOTH copies before writing this - but that was luck rather than design. It now names the good copy by checksum and the bad one to refuse, and says the thing that makes that usable: both print the same version string, so naming the version identifies nothing. Also landed: two rules about labels inside macros, pinned against the reference so they cannot drift.
detail: master b65eea87. Boot read now names 61e67256 (identical in skdisasm) to use and 0dee1f98 to refuse, with the shared guard asl_ref.sh whose selfcheck proves it refuses rather than claiming to. Corrected a figure I published: 'four binaries, one bad' was four PATHS, TWO PROGRAMS - one bad build of two. The label parcel: four asl-minted vectors + a refusal assertion, six runners repinned (not the three I briefed - the sweep globbed notes/*-probes/ and the align runners live under probes/), guard fires at status 3 against the varying build, one invalidated listing superseded in place not swapped. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 395 suites (independently counted), 4542/0/2, 0 skip, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, GREEN. No ROM byte moved - the whole crates/ diff is test code and doc comments.

headline: And the agent turned my own rule back on me: the measurement I handed it could not have answered the question I asked.
matters: I asked whether our assembler and the old one agree on a value, and warned that 'resolving is not agreeing'. Then I handed over a test case where the answer was zero - and zero is equally what three different failures produce. So my check could not have told agreement from any of them. The agent moved the test four bytes along, where the right answer is four and none of the failures produce it, and THEN established they agree. That is the exact rule I wrote into our reference document a few hours earlier, applied to my own work by someone who read it. It is the best outcome I could ask for from writing it down.

headline: The survey is done: 45 placement rules your engine relies on, and 19 of them are checked by nothing at all.
matters: This is the measurement item 14 was waiting on. The count is not the story - the distribution is. Of the 45 rules, 22 have a check somewhere, and of those 22, sixteen are checked by MY tool rather than by your engine's build. Only THREE hard placement checks live on the engine side, all of them for one game only, all skipped in a fast build, and two of the three rest on assumptions nothing verifies. Nineteen rules are checked by nothing anywhere. It also found that one of your engine's own room-checking tools CAN REPORT SUCCESS ON A REAL BREACH - it works out where the data ends by assuming a particular art file is last, and nothing checks that it is. Twelve of the 45 rules are that same mistake: a name standing in for a position. THE ANSWER to whether the frozen tables can be retired is NO, not yet, and for a structural reason rather than a missing checklist.
detail: master c70f9b1d. docs/superpowers/notes/2026-09-05-decouple-aeon-side-inventory.md, 45 constraints in 8 classes, each with source, anchor (symbol or SHA, never a line number), where-checked and what-lapses. Read at pinned aeon 9e3d2861 in a detached worktree. Per source: build side 24 rows, .emp ensures 8 of 1,246 sites, commit prose 7 rows from 4,434 commits with a genuine null. Positive control passed per source. Also found: aeon's live abs.w ceiling booking (9c8117ed) prescribes a VACUOUS check - it names a phased section's VMA not its LMA, so the grep always prints 8000 and no shrink can move it; real margin is 36 not zero, and aeon named that exact class four days later without back-applying it. Precondition priced: sweeping Art_Sonic +/-64KB, 2,773 of 131,073 positions fail in 43 forbidden bands, current margin 5,188 B. FOUR corrections to my brief, two to figures I published: the alignment predicates ARE implemented (4 of 7, not the 2 I reported - the names appear nowhere in sigil, my own name-vs-behaviour rule failing twice inside one measurement); staleness is 978 commits not 814 (814 measures to the frozen tip, the question is distance to current master - understated, the direction that never gets caught); the three-source scope omits map.toml prose, the densest source; and 'do not re-enumerate sigil' was wrong for the where-checked column. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 395 suites, 4542/0/2, GREEN.

headline: The copy of the old assembler we picked as the trustworthy one is not trustworthy either - it just lies the same way every time.
matters: Yesterday I found that two copies of the old assembler on this machine print an identical version banner and are different programs, and that one of them invents a fresh random number whenever it meets something it cannot work out. We pinned everything to the other copy. Today's measurement says the other copy does the same thing, and hides it better: when it cannot work out an operand it silently hands back THE LAST NUMBER IT HAPPENED TO CALCULATE, with no error at all. So the answer depends on what the lines above it were doing, and it gives you the same wrong number on every re-run - which is exactly what makes a person write it down as a measurement. The bad copy announces itself the second time you run it; the good copy never does. Neither is right, and we match neither. The decision to pin by fingerprint is unchanged and I am not walking it back - not knowing which program answered was always the worse problem. What changed is that pinning tells you WHICH program produced a number, and nothing at all about whether that number is real. This is the third time this week the project has found a wrong answer that produced no complaint whatsoever, which is the whole reason I no longer let a falling complaint-count stand as evidence of progress.
detail: master 59308883, docs/OVERSEER.md. Reproduced firsthand at this seat before ruling: d9.asm on md5 61e672562465725a8c102288a7da9098, three runs, exit 0 no diagnostic - three declined #f(<register>) immediates each preceded by a successful call holding $0111/$0222/$0333 return 0111/0222/0333, each echoing the line above, three distinct echoes. The uniform 0000 previously measured on d8 was the initial state of that slot, not a policy. Refutes the contrast the md5 ruling was banked with ('303C 8000 on every run of the reference build' against four random draws): I re-ran wrange.asm under the reference build and line 5 legitimately computes 8000 from #-32768, lines 6-9 being range-refused then echo it. Booked to ASL-SILENT-WRONG-ON-BOTH-BUILDS rather than fixed. Ruled under the autonomy directive's just-do-it clause (assembler internals, no language surface); logged because a reasonable person could have read the same data as 'the pin is working'.

headline: Every probe we run now checks WHICH copy of the old assembler answered it, and eight places that quoted a fake number are corrected.
matters: This closes the row I opened this morning. The mechanical half: 15 more of our probe scripts now refuse to run unless the assembler in front of them is the exact program we mean, instead of merely being pointed at the right file - and seven others deliberately keep a second copy, each printing which one it used. Along the way the list of scripts I had written down turned out to be wrong in BOTH directions, including two that took the assembler as an argument and printed nothing at all about it, so anything they produced said only that 'an assembler' had run. The half that matters more: when I found this morning that our trusted copy silently hands back a stale number, that made every place we had written such a number down suspect. There were eight, and all eight are corrected - including, awkwardly, the guard script's own explanation and the first paragraph of the document that teaches this rule. Finding all eight took four different ways of searching, and the search this project already had - does the text name the fingerprint or just the version? - could not see a single one of them, because those eight cited the fingerprint perfectly and still quoted a made-up number. Nothing in the game or the engine changes; this is about whether the numbers we measure against are real.
detail: master 2fb1b19e, merge of parcel/asl-md5-pin-residue (cfa5c39a). Re-verified ON THE MERGED TREE, not branch-side: selfcheck pass=6 fail=0; all 25 sourced-guard entry points at their expected disposition against the varying build (20 exit 3, five documented exceptions read in source); sweep 208 probes 0 UNSTABLE on the reference build, 22 UNSTABLE on the varying one; 2 pre-existing SIGSEGVs counted not swallowed; cargo check -p sigil-frontend-as --tests clean off a disk target dir, crate changes comment-only. Reproduced firsthand before landing: d9 (three declined #f(<reg>) echoing 0111/0222/0333, three runs, exit 0) and wcarry.asm, which is wrange.asm with ONLY line 5's accepted value changed $8000 -> $1234 and all four refused lines following - the positive discriminator, stronger than my own d9 reproduction, and it proves the loud range path and the silent function path leak identically. Also verified d1b firsthand: `if Undefined1=1` takes TRUE exactly as `Undefined1=0` does, so no numeric placeholder satisfies both and a refused condition is not evaluated against a substitute at all - the agent built that control to kill its own inviting hypothesis and committed it as the refutation. Agent's own process finding, its words: it had corrected characterise.sh mid-file and left the same sentence standing in that file's header and build table - fixing a file is not fixing every instance in it. Booked, not fixed: ASL-SILENT-WRONG-ON-BOTH-BUILDS; and gen_{m68k,z80}_vectors / gen_snippet_vectors take ASL_BIN with no default, no digest, and mint committed goldens carrying no provenance line - the worst-identified instruments in the tree, needing their own row since a digest pin would contradict the ratified P4d out-of-repo decision. Five notes from the same week state ground truth as the varying build cited by banner with no committed probe dir.

headline: Your engine lane checked my survey and caught me doing the exact thing the survey was complaining about.
matters: The survey said one of the engine's checks was using a stale, hand-written landmark instead of measuring. That was right. But when I gave the corrected number, I copied it from a note written six days earlier instead of measuring it myself - so the paragraph criticising a stale figure contained one. The real margin is 26 bytes, not the 36 I published, and the landmark I named is not even the binding one. Worth noticing which way the error went: 36 looks like MORE breathing room than 26, and a mistake in the comfortable direction is the one nobody goes looking for. Second thing they caught, and this one is good news: our own language already has a construct that machine-checks the exact kind of adjacency assumption five of my unchecked rows are about - it is used 47 times across 20 engine files. My survey never mentioned it. I checked whether that means I overcounted the problem and it does not: none of those five sites uses it. So the headline stands - 19 rules checked by nothing - but the fix for a third of the worst class is now much cheaper than I told you, because it needs no new mechanism invented, only those sites written in a form that already ships.
detail: master 72a37240. Appended as dated §7 to docs/superpowers/notes/2026-09-05-decouple-aeon-side-inventory.md rather than rewritten, so the corrections stay legible. aeon 305af222 verified firsthand as an ancestor of their origin/master before acting; text located by git show | grep nt_row. Defect 1 confirmed independently by aeon across all twelve rows, with a sharper framing than mine: Art_Sonic is the max-LMA label below the anchor with zero labels between, so the assumption holds by luck of declared order, not by construction. Defect 2: binding symbol is nt_row inside BG_Init at 0x801A, margin 26 B; Sound_PlaySFX at 0x825A with 602 B is not binding; BG_Init's body straddles 0x8000; neighbourhood is bg.emp/bg_anim.emp not the sound region; aeon replaced the named-symbol grep with an awk that measures. falls_into: 47 occurrences / 20 files, enforced in sigil crates/sigil-frontend-emp/src/corpus_contracts.rs. Measured that it does NOT move the count - none of the nine G1-G5 symbols appears in any falls_into declaration; source-side proc fallthrough vs gate-side data/routine layout, same shape different sites. I sent that correction back to the hub, since their relay's wording invited the overcounted reading. Also banked: P6 was NOT re-run by aeon and carries sigil's measurement alone; three further constraint sources (map.toml prose carries A9/A10, intra-section emission order is unexpressible in map.toml at all with page_cache.emp:926 live on it, decisions.jsonl is a fifth source with 50 cards); aeon's pytest lane structurally blind to placement - 20 placement-shaped files reading committed cuts of past listings - which corroborates §2 by a different enumeration parameter rather than echoing it.
